slides.0.title: Rum, tequila and mezcal
slides.0.subtitle: Sugarcane and agave: two tropical raw materials, two terroirs
slides.1.title: Rum
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Raw materials
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Most rum is made from molasses (a by-product of sugar making); rhum agricole uses fresh cane juice, with grassy, vegetal notes. Martinique’s rhum agricole has held an AOC since 1996
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Styles and colonial heritage
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Commonly grouped by colonial tradition: the Spanish tradition is lighter (column stills), the English richer (pot stills, such as Jamaica’s high-ester style), and the French is cane-juice agricole
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Regulatory differences
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Rum has no single global rulebook; rules on age, added sugar and colouring vary by country, so when recommending, explain origin and method rather than relying on age alone
slides.1.content: The first questions for any rum: molasses or cane juice? Pot or column?
slides.2.title: Tequila and mezcal
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Tequila: raw material and categories
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Only Blue Weber agave may be used, grown in Jalisco and parts of four other states; 100% agave uses only agave sugars, while mixto needs only at least 51%
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Age grades
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Blanco (unaged or very briefly rested), Reposado (2 months to under a year in wood), Añejo (at least 1 year in casks of up to 600 litres), Extra Añejo (at least 3 years)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Mezcal
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Mezcal can use many agave species (Espadín is most common), with Oaxaca the main region; traditionally the agave hearts are roasted in earthen pits with wood and stones, giving a distinct smokiness
slides.2.content: Tequila versus mezcal: variety restrictions, origin, and the smoke from pit roasting.
